---
title: "Writing an Analysis Plan"
description: "How the lab plans an analysis, and how to use the analysis-plan Claude skill to write your plan yourself and keep its milestones realistic."
---

Before you run an analysis in the lab, you write an analysis plan: what you'll
do to the data, in what order, with which thresholds, and why. You write it
yourself, even when the method is new to you. Writing it is how you learn the
method, and reading it is how Tomás sees what you understand and where you're
unsure, early enough to help. A plan someone else wrote can look finished while
hiding exactly those gaps, and you're the one who will defend it in a meeting
and debug the analysis later.

The `analysis-plan` skill turns Claude into a coach for this. It's available to
everyone in the lab's Claude organization. It sets up your plan as a Word
document, asks the questions that move each section forward, gives feedback on
what you write, and keeps your milestones and timeline realistic. It won't write
the science for you, on purpose.

Plans are working documents, not pre-registrations. They're expected to change.
What matters is that the changes are visible and that undecided choices are
written down instead of skipped.

## Before you start

- You need a seat in the lab's Claude organization (see
  [Welcome & First Steps](../onboarding/welcome.qmd)), and you should have read
  [AI Tools and Lab Data](../data/ai-tools-and-lab-data.qmd).
- Have these ready. Claude asks for whatever is missing, but the more you give
  it up front, the more useful the first version of the document is:
  - your question, in a sentence or two;
  - the dataset, and whether you already have access to it;
  - your role (undergraduate, IPRE, thesis, RA) and whether you've done this
    kind of analysis before;
  - how many hours a week you can give the project, and which weeks you'll have
    less time (exams, holidays);
  - the start date and how many weeks you have;
  - the end product: report, poster, thesis chapter, paper;
  - which day you meet Tomás.

## Starting a plan

Open a conversation in the lab organization, on [claude.ai](https://claude.ai)
or in Claude Code, and say what you want in plain words. Claude loads the skill
on its own. For example:

> I'm doing a summer IPRE with Tomás: 100 hours, starting 1 December. I want to
> test whether the association between plasma metabolites and cognitive decline
> differs by sex in ADNI. I have ADNI access but have never done metabolomics
> QC. We meet on Thursdays.

Claude replies with a Word document and a short message: where you need to
write, the two or three questions to answer first, and anything it assumed.
Keep the document in your project folder in the lab's OneDrive.

- **On claude.ai** there's nothing to install.
- **In Claude Code** you can also call the skill directly with
  `/analysis-plan`. It builds the document with Python, so you
  need `python-docx` (`pip install python-docx`). Start Claude Code in a folder
  that holds only your plan: not a data folder, and not a public repository.

### If Tomás gives you a starter plan

For some projects, Tomás sets up the plan before you start and gives you the
Word document. A starter plan made with the skill usually already has:

- the facts Tomás has settled for the project, marked *Given by the PI*: the
  aim, the dataset and where it lives, required covariates, a reference sample
  size;
- a yellow box of pointers in each section, for you to answer;
- a first set of milestones and a timeline, with the ones that need Tomás's
  sign-off marked.

Don't start a new plan. Attach the document to a conversation and say where it
came from, for example "Tomás gave me this starter plan for my project. Help me
work through it." Claude then works in that document:

- **The givens stay as they are.** If you think one is wrong or doesn't fit
  your data, don't change it: add it to the open questions with your proposal,
  and Tomás will decide.
- **The milestones get resized to your time.** They were sized from what Tomás
  expected. Tell Claude how many hours a week you actually have and which weeks
  will be lighter; the change goes in the change log.
- **Nothing gets overwritten.** Write your answers in Word or in the
  conversation. Either way, your words go in as you wrote them, and Claude
  doesn't rebuild the document, so neither Tomás's text nor yours is lost.

If the starter plan is a Word document Tomás wrote directly rather than one made
with the skill, tell Claude which parts Tomás wrote, so it treats them as
settled and coaches you on the rest. If it has no milestones yet, ask Claude to add
milestones and a timeline; they go at the end of the document.

## What's in the document

| Part | What it's for |
|---|---|
| Header | Author, PI, version, the time you have, and the end product |
| Readiness snapshot | Each section's level (see [Is it ready?](#is-it-ready)) and what would move it up |
| Background, Data, QC, Analysis | Your text. Each section has a yellow box of pointers: questions about *your* dataset and variables. Answer them in your own words above the box, then delete them. |
| Planned tables and figures | Empty versions of what you'll show: the sample flow, Table 1, the main results table and figure. You choose the rows and columns. |
| Key readings | Two to five references, each with a line on what to read it for |
| Milestones and timeline | What you'll have to show each week, sized to your hours |
| Open questions, decision log, change log | What's undecided, what was decided and why, and what changed in the plan |

The empty tables are there because designing Table 1 before running anything
forces the decisions that matter (which groups, which denominator, which
comparison) while they're still cheap to change.

Claude checks references with a literature tool when it has one and marks the
rest "to verify". Read a reference before you rely on it either way.

## How the coaching works

You write the science: the background and hypothesis; the QC steps, their
order, thresholds and reasons; the model and covariates; the multiple-testing
rule; and what you'll do with each possible result. Claude writes the structure,
the pointers, feedback on your text, and the milestone tables, which you confirm
or correct. Facts Tomás has already fixed for the project, such as the dataset
or a required covariate, appear marked *Given by the PI*.

When you're stuck, Claude helps one step at a time and stops as soon as you can
write:

1. a question that exposes the gap ("Two replicates of the same sample disagree.
   How would you decide whether that metabolite is still usable?");
2. the consideration to weigh, without resolving it;
3. where the answer lives, and what to look for there;
4. how a comparable step is written for a different kind of study, and why, so
   you can write the equivalent for yours.

If you're still stuck after that, that's useful information, not a failure. The
choice goes into the open questions, with your best attempt as the proposed
answer, for Tomás to look at.

Feedback is direct. If something is wrong, for example a Bonferroni correction
that divides by the number of participants instead of the number of tests,
Claude says so and asks the question that leads you to the fix.

If you're short on time and ask Claude to just write a section, it will ask you
for one rough sentence and react to that instead. A section honestly marked
*Sketch*, with its open questions listed, is fine to show Tomás, and more useful
than a polished one you didn't write.

## What to ask for

| When | Say something like | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| You're starting out | "Help me start my analysis plan for …" | The document, and the first few pointers to answer |
| Tomás gave you a starter plan | "Tomás gave me this starter plan. Help me work through it." (attach the file) | Coaching in that document: the givens stay, and the milestones are checked against your hours (see [above](#if-tomás-gives-you-a-starter-plan)) |
| You have a draft | "Is my plan ready to show Tomás?" (attach the file) | A level for each section, any errors stated plainly, and the three gaps that matter most. Your text isn't rewritten. |
| Every week | "Weekly check-in on my plan" (attach the file) | Updated milestones and timeline, and a draft of your weekly update |
| You already have a plan in Word | "Add milestones and a timeline to my plan" (attach it) | The tracking tables, added at the end of your own document |
| You're supervising a new student | "Set up a starter plan for a student working on …" | A scaffold with your facts as givens and pointers for the student to answer |

Claude doesn't remember earlier conversations, so attach the current version of
the Word file every time. Once you've edited the file yourself, Claude only
rewrites its tracking tables and leaves your text alone, so you can keep writing
in Word between sessions.

## Is it ready?

Each section of a plan gets one of four levels, based on what's on the page, not
on what you meant:

| Level | Means |
|---|---|
| Missing | Nothing, or just a heading |
| Sketch | Says what will be done in general terms, without thresholds, order, or reasons |
| Specific | Steps, variables and thresholds are named, and someone could mostly follow it; some reasons, counts or contingencies are missing |
| Ready | Another lab member could run the analysis from the plan without asking you anything |

Most first drafts are Sketch, and that's normal. You don't need Ready to show
the plan to Tomás. Show it once Background and Data are Specific and everything
you don't know yet is written down as an open question with your proposed
answer. An honest draft shown early is worth more than a polished one shown
late.

## What a finished plan has

The test is whether another lab member could run the analysis from the plan
alone. Finished plans in the lab:

- name the response and predictors concretely: variables, time points, units;
- number the steps in the order they'll be run, each one an action;
- give every filter a threshold and say what happens at the edges, such as a
  categorical variable with a level that's too small;
- give every threshold and choice a reason: a citation, a stated convention, or
  a calculation;
- track the sample size through the filters, ending in a final N by group;
- list the covariates by name, saying why each one is there and which ones vary
  by time point or model;
- write the model as an equation and name the software;
- count the tests and compute the significance threshold;
- say what happens next: if nothing is significant, how hits are followed up,
  and how results are replicated or checked with a second implementation;
- name the plots;
- show unresolved choices, with the options, instead of skipping them;
- say where the data and code live and how privacy is handled.

The difference between a sketch and a finished step, from the lab's EWAS and
PheWAS plans:

| Sketch | Finished |
|---|---|
| "We will QC the exposures." | "Require n ≥ 200. Binary or categorical: at least 50 per category; a dropped categorical returns only if its levels can be combined so each has 50, the levels still make sense, and it does not become binary. Continuous: fewer than 90% zeros; log-transform if the absolute skew is above 1." |
| "We will correct for multiple testing." | "64 phenotypes × (184 + 212) exposures = 25,344 results; SES exposures add 4,032. Prospective Bonferroni p = 0.05 / 29,376 = 1.70e-06." |
| "We will adjust for confounders." | "Non-varying: state, ethnicity, SES level, sex. Varying, taken at the phenotype time point: BMI, cotinine, caregiver education. SES is excluded as a covariate in models where the exposure is an SES variable." |
| "We will handle outliers." | "Identify outliers but do not remove them; report descriptive statistics with and without them to gauge their effect. Remove only physically impossible values." |
| (nothing about what's undecided) | "Undetermined follow-up, highlighted: if one exposure is significant at several time points, put them in one model; if some lose significance, likelihood-ratio test of the full against the reduced model." |

## Milestones and the timeline

A milestone is something you can show: a table, a figure, a decision, code that
runs, a document. "Read about QC" is an activity, and nobody can check an
activity. Each milestone has a *done when* that Tomás could verify in a minute,
an estimate in hours, a due week, and a status.

Claude proposes the milestones from the steps in your own plan, and you confirm
or correct them. They're sized from your hours:

- Only about 80% of your available hours are planned. The rest is buffer, and
  you will use it.
- There should be something to show at every check-in, so most milestones are 4
  to 15 hours of work.
- The first milestone is due in week one or two, is small, and touches the real
  data, for example N at baseline by sex and group. It brings out access and
  setup problems while they're cheap to fix.
- The plan itself is a milestone that Tomás signs off, and so is each decision
  before an expensive step, such as agreeing on QC thresholds or the primary
  model.
- A first attempt at anything (the cluster, a new tool) takes about twice what
  you'd guess.
- If the work doesn't fit, the estimates stay and the scope shrinks. What to cut
  becomes a question for Tomás, with your proposal.

The timeline is drawn from the milestones: one row per milestone, one column
per week, plus your check-ins and the hours available and planned each week.
Claude flags weeks with more work planned than hours available, milestones that
are too big, and long stretches with nothing to show.

Claude starts from the lab's usual time budgets. Your own numbers win.

| Who | Starting estimate |
|---|---|
| Undergraduate during the semester | 6 h/week in teaching weeks, none in exam weeks |
| University-wide IPRE | Usually 100 hours in total. Summer round: setup and reading in December, the analysis in January, only report writing in February. Winter round: the analysis in July, finishing and writing the report in August. |
| Engineering IPre | The course credits are the weekly hours: 10 credits is about 10 h/week |

The university is closed in February, so nothing your project depends on is
planned for then. IPRE hours and report deadlines change from round to round, so
check the rules for yours.

## Weekly check-ins

Before you meet Tomás, attach your current plan and ask Claude for a check-in.
It asks what you finished, what you can show, what took longer than expected,
what's blocked, and how many hours you actually worked. A milestone is Done
when its *done when* is met, so expect to be asked for the result or its
headline numbers.

If a milestone slips by a week and nothing depends on it, it moves and the
change log records it. If a slip eats the buffer or pushes back the end product,
Claude doesn't squeeze everything else to make it fit. It writes the options
(cut this, or move that) as an open question for Tomás, with your proposal.

The check-in ends with a draft of your weekly update, in your voice, for Zulip or
[lab meeting](../lab-life/lab-meetings.qmd). It reports rather than spins: if
nothing got finished, it says so.

```
Week 4 update: [project]
Done: M3 sample-flow table (7 h, planned 7)
To show: [file or link]
Slipped: M4 Table 1, half done; exams took 4 of my 10 h
Blocked: Q2 needs an answer before M5
Next: finish M4, start M5
Questions for Tomás: Q2 [question] (my proposal: [proposal])
```

## Open questions and decisions

Every choice you haven't settled goes in the open-questions table, with what it
blocks and your proposed answer. A question with a proposal takes Tomás a
minute to answer; a bare question takes a meeting, and writing the proposal is
where you do the thinking. Once a question is answered, it moves to the decision
log with the date, the reason, and who decided. Changing the plan is expected;
the log is there so it never changes silently.

## Data and privacy

The plan describes your data; it never contains it. In the conversation, counts
and summary statistics are fine, such as N by sex and diagnosis or a
missingness rate. Participant-level rows are not: ADNI and similar datasets are
under data use agreements, so never paste individual records into Claude. If
you think you did, tell Tomás right away. See
[AI Tools and Lab Data](../data/ai-tools-and-lab-data.qmd) for what can go into
which tool, and keep the plan in the lab's OneDrive, not in a public repository.
